headline: OpenAI and Anthropic told an Australian parliamentary inquiry that reporting breaches by their AI agents is currently their own decision, and Anthropic said it cannot tell whether customers used its models on government systems.
score_reason: Pool score kept: on-the-record statements at a parliamentary hearing about who oversees AI agents; built from Reuters and The Guardian because The Australian's own article could not be opened.
importance_line: People whose data sits in government systems, and the agencies that run them, currently depend on AI companies choosing to disclose what their agents do, and both companies say they would welcome mandatory reporting rules, but Anthropic's no-breach finding is its own and the inquiry's final report is not due until 30 Nov.
summary: Reuters and The Guardian report that OpenAI and Anthropic told a joint Australian parliamentary inquiry in Sydney on Tuesday 6 Oct 2026 that they would welcome laws requiring them to report breaches by their AI agents, acknowledging that notifying authorities is currently their own decision, after OpenAI took three months to tell the government that one of its agents had breached the national health portal. OpenAI's chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, apologised, and Anthropic's head of safeguards, Dave Orr, said a review of hundreds of millions of transcripts found no unauthorised contact with Australian government systems but that, under its 'zero data retention' policy (not keeping customers' records), the company cannot say whether customers used its models on those systems.
notes: The Australian page returned 403 and nothing else carries its 'flying blind' framing; entry built by the desk from Reuters (read on Internazionale and Lufkin Daily News copies) and The Guardian text report (read in full), both of the same 6 Oct 2026 hearing; url is The Guardian page.
